terms.definition: learning from data that has NO answer column: the algorithm looks for structure (groups, oddities) on its own.
a third kind of learning, where a program learns by trying actions and getting rewards (Chapter 18); not used here.
learning what normal data looks like, then flagging the instances that do not fit it.
an instance that does not look like the rest of the data (also called an outlier).
a normal instance — the opposite of an outlier.
estimating how the data is spread over the space: which regions are crowded and which are nearly empty.
how crowded a region of the data is: many instances packed close together = high density; a lonely instance = low density.
a description of which values are likely and which are rare; the chances of all possible values add up to 1.
grouping customers by behaviour so each group can be treated differently.
learning when only a few instances have labels and most have none.
splitting an image into regions (segments) whose pixels belong together.
turning a table with many columns into one with fewer columns while keeping the useful information (Chapter 8's subject).
the centre of a cluster: the average position of its instances (average of each column).
a classic table of 150 flowers of 3 species, with 4 measurements each (sepal and petal length and width, in cm).
groups nested inside bigger groups.
a Scikit-Learn function that generates points gathered in round clumps (blobs) around chosen centres; handy test data.
fit the model, then return its prediction for each training row, in one call.
after k-means is fitted: one cluster NUMBER per training instance (0, 1, 2 ...). An arbitrary bucket number, not a real-world label.
cutting the plane into regions, one per centroid, where every point belongs to the region of its nearest centroid.
giving each instance exactly one cluster.
giving each instance a score (a distance or a probability) for EVERY cluster, instead of one cluster.
a solution that no small change can improve, even though a completely different solution would be better.
to settle: repeating the steps stops changing anything.
the starting values an algorithm begins from (for k-means: where the k centroids start).
k-means' score: add up, over all instances, the squared distance from each one to its own centroid. Lower = tighter clusters.
how many times k-means is run from different random starts; the run with the lowest inertia is kept.
a smarter way to place the starting centroids: one at a time, each new one more likely to land far from the ones already placed.
going straight from A to C is never longer than going from A to B and then to C.
a small random chunk of rows processed in one step, instead of the whole dataset at once.
the bend in a curve where the steep part meets the flat part.
a score from -1 to +1 for each instance: how much closer it is to its own cluster than to the next-nearest cluster; averaged over all instances it scores a whole clustering.
a number with no units (not metres, not pixels), so it can be compared across datasets.
round: spread the same amount in every direction (in 2D, a circle).
a stretched circle; elliptical clusters are longer in one direction than in another and may be tilted.
one dot of an image. A colour pixel is 3 numbers: red, green and blue intensity, each 0 to 255.
red, green, blue: the 3 numbers (channels) that describe one pixel's colour.
change an array's shape (rows × columns) without changing its numbers; -1 means "work this size out for me".
a kind of neural network built for images (Chapter 14).
representing many values by a small set of representative values (a codebook); for an image, redrawing it with a small palette of colours.
1,797 small 8 × 8 grey images of handwritten digits 0 to 9 that ship with Scikit-Learn (64 pixel columns each).
despite its name, a simple CLASSIFICATION model (Chapter 4): it outputs a probability per class.
how correct results are; for a classifier, the share of test instances it gets right (0.84 = 84%).
the training instance closest to a cluster's centroid: the most typical member of that cluster.
copying a known label onto other, unlabeled instances — here, onto every member of the same cluster.
a loop where the model asks a human to label the instances that would help it most, then retrains.
the active-learning rule: ask the human about the instances the current model is least sure about.
a clustering algorithm that defines a cluster as a connected region where instances are packed densely; it finds any shape and marks leftovers as anomalies.
the Greek letter ε; in DBSCAN, the radius: how close two instances must be to count as neighbours.
all the instances within distance ε of a given instance.
in DBSCAN, an instance with at least min_samples instances (itself included) within distance ε: it sits in a dense region.
DBSCAN's other setting: how many instances an ε-neighborhood must hold for its centre to be a core instance.
a toy dataset of two interlocking crescent (half-moon) shapes.
a classifier that labels a new instance by majority vote of its k nearest training instances.
a model that assumes the data was generated by a few bell-shaped (Gaussian) clouds, each with its own centre, shape and share of the data.
for one Gaussian cloud: the numbers that set how wide it is in each direction and how it is tilted (the shape of its ellipse).
a number saying how much something counts; for a Gaussian mixture, the share of the data each cloud produced (the weights add up to 1).
a number from 0 to 1 saying how likely something is (0.98 = 98% likely).
the algorithm that fits a Gaussian mixture: guess the clouds, then repeat two steps — work out each instance's probabilities, then re-fit every cloud — until nothing changes.
EM's first step: with the current clouds, work out the probability that each instance came from each cloud.
EM's second step: re-fit every cloud's centre, shape and weight from ALL instances, each counted by its probability.
in EM, the probability that one instance belongs to one cluster, given the current clouds.
a model of how the data was produced, so it can also make up new instances (gm.sample).
returns, for each instance, the LOG of the density the fitted model puts at that point: high = normal, very low = unusual.
a normal item wrongly flagged (a good product called defective).
a real problem the detector misses (a defect that slips through).
flag more and you catch more real anomalies (recall) but also raise more false alarms (worse precision); flag less, the reverse (Chapter 3).
like anomaly detection, but the training data is assumed clean; the question is whether a NEW instance is unlike everything seen.
a score that rewards fitting the data well but charges for every parameter the model learned; lower is better.
Bayesian information criterion: fit penalty plus log(m) per parameter; lowest wins.
Akaike information criterion: fit penalty plus 2 per parameter; lowest wins.
how plausible the model's fitted numbers make the data you actually observed; fitting tries to make it as large as possible.
a Gaussian mixture that is given too many clusters on purpose and pushes the weights of unneeded ones to about 0.
a detector that fits ONE Gaussian ellipse to the normal data while ignoring likely outliers (Scikit-Learn: EllipticEnvelope).
a detector that cuts the data with random splits; instances cut off from the rest after very few splits are flagged.
a detector that compares how crowded an instance's neighbourhood is with how crowded its neighbours' neighbourhoods are.
a novelty detector that draws a boundary around the (clean) training data; anything outside is new.
the chapter's other clustering algorithms, named in the exercises: agglomerative clustering, BIRCH, mean-shift, spectral clustering (the book covers them briefly).
principal component analysis (Chapter 8): shrinks a table to fewer columns while keeping most of its spread.
undo a transformation: e.g. turn PCA's few columns back into the original number of columns (approximately).
how far the rebuilt (inverse-transformed) data is from the original: the average squared gap.
a dataset of 400 grey 64 × 64 photos of 40 people's faces (10 each), used in the exercises.
